newsitem.title: USA: Insurer Phoenix courts women's pro basketball.
newsitem.headline: Insurer Phoenix courts women's pro basketball.

text.p: What does a fledgling women's basketball league have to do with the rather stodgy business of selling life insurance?
Quite a bit, according to Robert Fiondella, chairman and chief executive of Phoenix Home Life Mutual Insurance Co.
Phoenix, the nation's ninth-biggest mutual life insurer, is leading a full-court press to assist the American Basketball League (ABL) in hitting the big time.
The Hartford-based company recently spent $3 million to buy a 20 percent ownership in the ABL, whose nine teams across the United States will begin their second season in October.
The ABL competes against the WNBA -- a newer, glitzier women's league that plays a 28-game summer season and has the marketing might of the men's NBA (National Basketball Association) behind it.
"There is a very solid business reason for us to pursue this -- although most people would wonder," Fiondella said.
He is not worried about competition from the WNBA, he said, and he is convinced the ABL will prove a viable, long-term investment.
Phoenix's investment includes the option to acquire the team operating rights to the ABL's New England Blizzard.
The Blizzard, coached by former Boston Celtics great K.C. Jones, plays half its home games in Hartford and the other half in nearby Springfield, Mass.
"We believe women have been underserved in terms of financial service and financial planning, and we have decided to target that market," Fiondella said.
In addition to its sponsorship of the ABL, Phoenix has created a summer internship programme to train league players in insurance careers, once their playing days end.
The six-week course drew five of the ABL's 80 players, including Tara Davis of the Seattle Reign and Lauretta Freeman of the Atlanta Glory.

The paid internship provides classroom training and also allows students to shadow Phoenix financial advisers in the field for a firsthand look at customer interaction and what it takes to succeed in the insurance business.
"The insurance market for women is growing dramatically faster than the insurance market for men," said Nathaniel Brinn, vice president of strategic development for Phoenix.
"We want more women in our sales force, frankly," Brinn said. Only a small number of Phoenix's several thousand agents are women.
Fiondella said that women basketball players possess the same qualities as successful insurance professionals -- including discipline, tenacity and coping with rejection.
Phoenix views the ABL as a more targeted and effective vehicle for building brand awareness than traditional advertising.

"We could have put $3 million (instead) into passive advertising, and maybe not even end up in the same place. At least with the ABL, we think there's a reasonable probability it's going to be very successful."

Phoenix thinks its timing is good. The popularity of women's basketball in the United States has surged since the Women Huskies of the University of Connecticut went undefeated to win the NCAA championship in 1995.
Fiondella said he is convinced the ABL will flourish because it has better players, a longer season, and more substance than the strongly hyped WNBA.
"People were concerned that maybe the WNBA would overwhelm the ABL in player signings, but it was really the reverse. Because the ABL represents a movement, not simply a merchandising opportunity."
In its first year, the ABL signed 10 of the country's top 13 women players, Brinn said. The average ABL salary of $70,000 is well above that of the WNBA, he said.

Phoenix, with assets under management of $40 billion, owns 8 percent of reinsurer PXRE Corp. It also owns approximately 30 percent of international money manager Aberdeen Asset Management Ltd, and 60 percent of money manager Phoenix Duff & Phelps Corp.
